title.heading:
Building the
rbmod carrier
title.text:
A rev 1 board, five modules and the rework.
11 steps with a soldering iron.

say.text: Building the R B mod carrier of the R C bench: a revision 1 board, five modules and the rework, in 11 steps.

labels.title: rbmod carrier
labels.text: Under the display, modules up. The display leaves the modules little height.

chips.text: Wire GPIO 15 to R1's outer pad

labels.title: R1 to R8 stay empty
labels.text: Eight footprints for 120 Ω. A track joins the two pads of each.

labels.title: J6 sits on the back
labels.text: The only part on the other side of the board.

labels.title: What goes on the board
labels.text: 5 modules on straight 2.54 mm pin strips, 2 angled 3 x 4 pin headers, 6 JST PH connectors, 1 Mini-Fit Jr, a 3 V zener and 4.7 kΩ. For the rework: a wire, 2.2 kΩ and a 5.6 V zener.

labels.title: PROGP03 runs to GPIO 26
labels.text: GPIO 26 is an ADC pin and not 5 V tolerant. A Hitec or KST servo pulls the programming line up to its supply. Do this first, while the board is bare.

labels.title: Scratch the track open at R1
labels.text: Between the two pads of R1, the end footprint of the row, next to J1 pin 1. Afterwards the two pads must not conduct to each other.

labels.title: D1 and R9: the TAP input
labels.text: D1 is a 3 V zener, its banded end on the square pad. R9 is 4.7 kΩ. Both lie flat on the board and are soldered on the back.

labels.title: JST PH and Mini-Fit Jr
labels.text: J3, J4, J5, J7 and J9 on the right edge and J8 on the left: on the module side, soldered on the back.

labels.title: J6 goes on the back
labels.text: A 4-pin JST PH, soldered from the module side.

labels.title: J1 and J2: angled 3 x 4 headers
labels.text: The pins point out over the board edge, towards the case wall. J1 carries the programming ports, J2 the servo outputs. Soldered on the back.

labels.title: M1 · RP2350-CAN
labels.text: The USB-C socket at the board edge. 2 x 20 pins: solder each on the module, then turn the board and solder each on the back.

labels.title: M8 and M7: the same way
labels.text: On pin strips with the plastic between: four pin pairs each and M7's EN pin, soldered on both sides. M8 makes the IOmcu's 5 V. M7 makes the 5 V of the programming ports and is switched through EN.

labels.title: M5 · INA3221
labels.text: On an 8-pin strip, the plastic between, soldered on both sides.

labels.title: M6 · USB-C PD trigger
labels.text: Its two large holes the same way: bare wire through both boards, filled with solder. Set its DIP switch to 15 V.

labels.title: Wire GPIO 15 to the outer pad
labels.text: From the module's pad 20, GP15, to the pad of R1 that leads on to J1. GPIO 26 ends at the inner pad and stays unused.

labels.title: 2.2 kΩ from EN to GND
labels.text: On top of the module, from EN to the GND pad beside it. An open EN reads as on: the pull-down keeps the ports' 5 V off while the IOmcu is in reset, in BOOTSEL or unpowered.

labels.title: 5.6 V zener from OUT+ to GND
labels.text: A 2 W or 5 W part on top of the module, its banded end, the cathode, on OUT+. A braking servo feeds energy back into the 5 V, and M7 latches off above about 6.0 V. The zener takes that energy.

insets.title: Modules sit on the strip's plastic
insets.text: Straight pin strips, the plastic between module and carrier: without it the through-hole parts can short out. The pins are soldered on both sides, on top of the module and on the back of the carrier. Press the module down level: the display leaves little headroom.

insets.title: Large holes: wire and solder
insets.bad: soldered on the module and on the back
insets.text: The 9 large holes carry the supply currents. Each takes a piece of bare wire through module and carrier and is filled with solder.

say.text: This is the bare R B mod carrier, seen from the module side. The eight resistor footprints stay empty. One connector, J 6, sits on the back.

You need five modules on straight pin strips, two angled pin headers, the connectors, a 3 volt zener diode and a 4.7 kilo ohm resistor. For the rework: a wire, a 2.2 kilo ohm resistor and a 5.6 volt zener diode.
Step 1. On this board, programming port 3 runs to G P I O 26, which is not 5 volt tolerant. Open that track while the board is bare.
Scratch the track open between the two pads of R 1, the end footprint next to J 1. Then check that the two pads no longer conduct.
Step 2. Fit the 3 volt zener diode D 1, with its band on the square pad, and the 4.7 kilo ohm resistor R 9. Solder both on the back.
Step 3. Fit the J S T connectors on the right edge and the power connector J 8 on the left, and solder them on the back. J 6 goes on the back of the board.
Step 4. Fit the two angled pin headers, J 1 and J 2, with their pins pointing out over the board edge.

Step 5. The modules sit on straight pin strips, with the plastic between module and carrier. Without the plastic, the through hole parts can short out. Solder every pin on both sides: on top of the module and on the back of the carrier. Press each module down level, because the display leaves little headroom.
Start with the R P 23 50 can module, its U S B socket at the board edge.
Step 6. The two buck modules go on the same way. M 7 also needs its enable pin.
Step 7. The I N A 3221 module sits on an 8 pin strip.
Its nine large holes carry the supply currents. Push a piece of bare wire through module and carrier, and fill each hole with solder on both sides.
Step 8. The U S B C, P D trigger gets the same wire and solder in its two large holes. Set its dip switch to 15 volts.
Step 9. Now the rework wire. Solder it from pad 20 of the module, G P 15, to the outer pad of R 1.
Step 10. Solder 2.2 kilo ohm on top of M 7, from the enable pad to the ground pad beside it. It keeps the 5 volts of the programming ports off until the controller switches them on.
Step 11. Solder the 5.6 volt zener diode on top of M 7, from the output to ground, with its band on the output pad. It takes the energy that a braking servo feeds back.
